sentences.text: Bajadasaurus is a genus of dinosaur belonging to the family Dicraeosauridae, a group of large, four-legged herbivores with long necks and tails but relatively small heads.
Its most striking feature is a set of extremely elongated, two-pronged neural spines extending from its neck vertebrae, which curve forward rather than backward.
One preserved neck vertebra possesses a neural spine measuring 58 centimeters in length, making the entire bone four times taller than it is long.
The animal had a lower jaw that was approximately 80 percent the length of its skull.
As of 2019, the Bajadasaurus skull was the most complete dicraeosaurid skull known to science.
The genus name Bajadasaurus combines the Spanish word bajada, referring to the specific site, with the Greek term saurus meaning lizard.
Analysis of the neural spines reveals they are highly vascularized and display cyclical growth marks, indicating rapid bone development.
Research estimates that Bajadasaurus replaced its teeth on average every 40.7 days.
The only known specimen, cataloged as MMCh-PV 75, was excavated in 2010 by paleontologists from the Argentinian National Scientific and Technical Research Council.

This holotype specimen, consisting of an almost complete skull, proatlas, atlas neuroapophyses, axis, and a tentatively identified fifth cervical vertebra, was found at the Bajada Colorada locality, 40 kilometers south of Picún Leufú near the Limay River.
The exposure of the eye openings suggests the animal could look forward while feeding.
Researchers suggest the spines may have supported a neck sail used for display or to deter rivals.
Muscle reconstruction indicates Bajadasaurus was less capable of pulling its head upward compared to the sauropod Camarasaurus.
A 2023 study suggests the animal may have possessed a keratinous beak-like structure supporting its tooth-bearing muzzle, though definitive evidence is missing.
However, a 2022 study argues that the spines likely did not support a keratinous sheath, contradicting earlier beliefs.
While several functions have been proposed for similar spines in related dinosaurs, a 2019 description suggests they served as passive defense in both Bajadasaurus and Amargasaurus.
Bajadasaurus belongs to the family Dicraeosauridae, which is one of the three principal families within the sauropod subdivision Diplodocoidea.
The genus is classified within the parent group Dicraeosaurinae.
A 2020 study by Whitlock and Mantilla placed Bajadasaurus as the most basal member of a specific clade within Dicraeosauridae, differing from earlier classifications.

Bajadasaurus lived in northern Patagonia, Argentina, during the Early Cretaceous between 145 and 132.9 million years ago, specifically from the Berriasian to the Valanginian stages, approximately 139.1 to 132.6 million years ago.
Fossils were recovered from the Bajada Colorada Formation, where sediments were mostly deposited by braided rivers in a fluvial and deltaic ecosystem.

The locality yielded remains of other sauropods, including Leinkupal laticauda and Ninjatitan zapatai, as well as theropods belonging to basal Tetanurae and possibly abelisauroids and deinonychosaurians.
